segments.voice: Yesterday, year 3 closed with the Gita's promise: no effort begun on this path is lost. Year four begins with the goddess.

A king rides into a forest alone, his kingdom lost. Enemies beat him in battle, then his own ministers turned on him and took the treasury. He tells himself he's out hunting. He finds the quiet hermitage of a sage named Medhas, and stays. And under the trees he can't stop worrying. Is my elephant fed? Are my servants treated well? Is my treasure being wasted? Then he meets a merchant named Samadhi, sitting there just as lost. That's how the Devi Mahatmya begins, and year four reads it whole.
screen: `A KING RIDES INTO A FOREST ALONE.` → `HE CAN'T STOP WORRYING.` → `A MERCHANT, JUST AS LOST.`

segments.voice: Devi Mahatmya means the glory of the goddess. Tradition places it inside a larger book, the Markandeya Purana, and it's also called the Chandi; in some homes and temples it's recited from beginning to end. Yet it opens with no goddess at all. Just two men with a problem. The merchant's is the harder one. His own wife and sons, greedy for his money, threw him out. And still he can't stop wondering whether they're well. So they bring the sage one honest question. In paraphrase: we know these things have left us. So why do we still grieve? Why doesn't knowing help? Medhas doesn't call them foolish. He points at birds: hungry themselves, they still drop grain into the beaks of their young. Every creature, he says, is pulled this way. Then he names the pull: Mahamaya, the great illusion, and in this text she is the goddess herself. She seizes the minds of even the wise and drags them into confusion. And the same goddess, when gracious, sets people free. That's the surprise. The goddess first appears not as a warrior but as the power inside the very worry these men carried into the forest. The king asks: who is this goddess? Medhas answers with stories, and the rest of the book is those stories.
screen: `TWO MEN WITH A PROBLEM.` · `WHY DOESN'T KNOWING HELP?` · `BIRDS FEEDING THEIR YOUNG.` · `MAHAMAYA BINDS, AND SETS FREE.` · then, large: `WHO IS THIS GODDESS?`

segments.voice: Let one thing your mind keeps going back to come up on its own, a person, a place, something gone that still pulls, and notice the pull the way the merchant noticed his, without arguing or fixing. With each breath out, let the grip loosen a little, keeping the care underneath; if you pray, hold it before God or the goddess in your own words, and if you don't, let the breath do the holding. If that pull is ever too heavy to carry alone, please reach out: in the US you can call or text 988, or call local emergency help.

howItsDone: Some Hindus recite the Devi Mahatmya, also called the Chandi or Durga Saptashati, from beginning to end, especially during Navaratri, and it is recited in some temples devoted to the goddess.
